steelman: For the well-defined class of constrained combinatorial and mathematical optimization problems where a verified solver already exists (LP, MIP, CP), the right engineering allocation in 2026 is to use the LLM as a formalizer (natural language to variables, constraints, objective) and to route the actual search to a classical solver, not to ask the agent to be the optimizer. This is a comparative-advantage claim, not a claim about model ceilings: the LLM's edge is turning messy human specs into a formal model; the solver's edge is producing a verifiable, near-optimal solution with a correctness guarantee no stochastic generator provides. Two independent 2026 benchmarks converge on this same prescription. FrontierOR finds the strongest one-shot model beats Gurobi on both quality and efficiency in only 31 percent of cases, and even strong coding agents with test-time evolution top out near 50 percent on hard tasks. A separate group's CP-SynC-XL benchmark (100 problems, 4,577 instances) finds that prompting the LLM to optimize search yields only 1.03 to 1.12x median speed-ups with a strongly bimodal effect (many instances slow down, correctness degrades on a long tail), and explicitly concludes you should use the LLM primarily to formalize for verified solvers. The convergence of two independently sourced origins on one architectural lesson (separate formalization from solving) is the load-bearing evidence.
strongest_attack: The ages-out attack: these are point-in-time snapshots of a fast-moving capability curve. The 31 percent and 50 percent figures are 2026 numbers; frontier models improve on a roughly annual cadence, so a next-generation model could plausibly cross Gurobi on a majority of cases and the whole thesis dissolves into a stale benchmark leaderboard. If the real content is only 'today's models lose to a 40-year-old solver,' the claim carries a short expiry and says nothing durable; a practitioner reading it in twelve months would be misled into keeping a solver in the loop that the model has since obsoleted. Under this framing the thesis is not false but perishable, which for an architectural recommendation is nearly as bad.
reconciliation: The attack lands only against the weak reading (models are currently bad at optimizing) and misses the strong reading the evidence actually supports. The CP-SynC-XL result is the tell: prompting a better model to optimize search did not help monotonically; it broke a long tail and dropped correctness. That is a structural signature, not a skill gap that scales away. A verified solver offers optimality and feasibility guarantees plus auditability that a probabilistic next-token generator cannot offer at any capability level, and even in the limit where a model matched solver quality it would still be more expensive, less reproducible, and unverifiable per run. So the durable claim is about division of labor exploiting a permanent asymmetry (verifiable search versus fluent formalization), not about a capability gap waiting to close. The attack does force a boundary: the thesis must be stated as a comparative-advantage and verifiability claim, and it must concede that the raw quality gap will narrow. Stated that way it survives, because narrowing the gap does not remove the reasons to keep the solver as the solver. The competing trivial-truism attack (do not use a general tool for a specialized job) also fails: the industry default being sold in 2026 is precisely just ask the agent, and the specific empirical shape (bimodal slowdown, correctness loss on a tail, 31 percent win rate) is a surprising, falsifiable, actionable finding that could have come out the other way.
strengthened_argument: For constrained optimization problems with a verifiable solver, keep the LLM as translator and the classical solver as optimizer, because the split exploits a durable asymmetry rather than a temporary capability gap: solvers give optimality and feasibility guarantees plus per-run auditability that a stochastic model does not, while LLMs excel at formalizing human specs into models. The empirical case is two independent 2026 origins converging on the same prescription: FrontierOR (best one-shot model beats Gurobi on both axes in only 31 percent of cases, agents near 50 percent on hard tasks) and CP-SynC-XL (100 problems, 4,577 instances; only 1.03 to 1.12x median speed-up from LLM-directed search, bimodal with a correctness-dropping long tail; recommendation to use the LLM to formalize for verified solvers). The claim explicitly concedes the raw quality gap will narrow with model progress, and shows why that does not invalidate the architecture: the CP-SynC-XL long-tail correctness failure is a structural property of asking a generator to do verified search, and even a model that matched solver quality would remain costlier, less reproducible, and unverifiable. The falsifiable core: if a future model both beats solvers on a majority of these problems AND provides equivalent per-run correctness guarantees at comparable cost, the thesis is refuted; the two benchmarks are the current evidence that this has not happened and that naively prompting the model to optimize actively breaks cases.
reason: The thesis is true on current evidence, falsifiable (named benchmarks with concrete win rates and a stated refutation condition), and non-trivial (it contradicts the live just ask the agent default and rests on a surprising bimodal, correctness-degrading empirical result). The strongest attack (ages out within a release cycle) narrows the claim to a comparative-advantage and verifiability argument but does not win, because the verified-solver guarantee and the long-tail correctness failure are structural, not artifacts of present capability; two independent origins converging on one architectural prescription is the load-bearing support. Verdict defensible.
